name: The Maples of Hugo Conwentz

location.address: Park Oliwski im. Adama Mickiewicza, Oliwa, Gdansk

access: Free, public park (11.3 ha, listed historic monument), open daily in daylight hours
transport: Oliwa district; about a 12 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the pair: two field maples side by side, the larger 245 centimetres round and 19.5 metres tall, the smaller 180 centimetres and 17. Designated in February 2026, the newest natural monument in Gdansk.
story:
Gdansk's newest protected tree is not one tree but two. On 26 February 2026 the city council entered a pair of field maples standing side by side in Park Oliwski onto Poland's register of natural monuments under a single record, the most recent designation on a city roll of 157 protected trees. The larger has a trunk 245 centimetres round and stands 19.5 metres; its companion measures 180 centimetres and 17 metres. Field maple is a slow, modest species that rarely gets big, and 245 centimetres is a considerable size for it, which puts these two somewhere around 150 to 200 years old. That figure comes from the trunk rather than from a document: no planting record has turned up.

The name is the other half of it. The register calls them Klony Hugo Conwentza, the Maples of Hugo Conwentz, after the botanist who ran this city's provincial museum and who is widely credited with founding the world's first state conservation agency, the Prussian office for the care of natural monuments, in 1906. The category these two maples have just been entered under is the one his office existed to administer. What the register does not say is why these particular trees carry his name. If you know, tell us.

name: The Ginkgo of Park Oliwski
age_estimate: not documented; a mature specimen, likely planted when the park's dendrological garden was developed in the 19th or early 20th century

location.address: Park Oliwski im. Adama Mickiewicza, Oliwa, Gdansk

access: Free, public park (11.3 ha, listed historic monument), open daily in daylight hours
transport: Oliwa district; about a 12 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped leaves, unlike anything else here, and by the trunk, 201 centimetres round. It stands in the old dendrological corner beside a European larch and a Weymouth pine registered the same day.
story:
For about a week each autumn this tree empties itself. Ginkgos turn uniformly gold and then drop the whole crown almost at once, sometimes inside two days, and for that week the ground underneath it is the reason to come.

The rest of the year it is a straight, quiet tree with a trunk 201 centimetres round and 20 metres of height, standing in the corner of Park Oliwski that was worked up into a dendrological collection. Poland entered it on the central register of natural monuments on 15 March 1992 as number 833, the same day it registered the European larch and the Weymouth pine growing a few paces away.

Ginkgo biloba is the last species of an entire order of plants. Its relatives were widespread before flowering trees existed and then disappeared everywhere except a corner of China, and the species survives now largely because people kept planting it, which is exactly what happened here. Nobody wrote down when. The girth reads like a nineteenth or early twentieth century planting rather than anything ancient, but that is a judgement about a trunk, not a record, and we have found no document either way. If you know when this one went in, tell us.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the whole crown turns gold and drops within days

name: The Cucumber Magnolia of Park Oliwski
age_estimate: not documented; an unusually large specimen of this species for the climate

location.address: Park Oliwski im. Adama Mickiewicza, Oliwa, Gdansk

access: Free, public park (11.3 ha, listed historic monument), open daily in daylight hours
transport: Oliwa district; about a 12 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad crown over a trunk 271 centimetres round, and by the cucumber-shaped green fruit in late summer. It is the larger of the two tree magnolias in Park Oliwski; the other is 250 metres away.
story:
Most people picture a magnolia as a garden shrub holding up pink goblets in April. This one is 19 metres tall with a trunk 271 centimetres round.

Magnolia acuminata is a forest tree from eastern North America, and it is called the cucumber tree for its unripe fruit, a knobbly green cylinder a few centimetres long that reddens through late summer. Its flowers are the anticlimax of the genus: greenish yellow, held high in the crown, easy to stand underneath and miss completely. What the species does instead is get big, and this specimen has done it a long way north of anywhere it grows wild.

It went onto Poland's register of natural monuments on 15 March 1992 as number 837. A second cucumber tree, 212 centimetres round, stands about 250 metres away in the same park, and the survey of Gdansk's protected trees picks out the tree magnolias of Park Oliwski, the ones past two metres of girth, as one of the collection's standouts. For a species that is only ever planted here as an ornamental, that is a real distinction.

Nobody has dated it. There is no planting record, and no growth rate published for the species at this latitude to work one out from. If you have found either, tell us.

name: The Three-Trunked Katsura of Park Oliwski
age_estimate: not documented; likely a late-19th or early-20th-century planting, since the species only reached European gardens after 1865

location.address: Park Oliwski im. Adama Mickiewicza, Oliwa, Gdansk

access: Free, public park (11.3 ha, listed historic monument), open daily in daylight hours
transport: Oliwa district; about a 12 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the three trunks splitting low out of one tree, 168, 189 and 158 centimetres round, carried up to 25 metres. It stands in the old dendrological corner of Park Oliwski.
story:
In October this tree smells of caramel. Katsura leaves give off a scent as they yellow and fall, variously described as burnt sugar, toffee or gingerbread, strong enough on a still afternoon that people look around for a bakery. It is one of the few trees you can find with your nose.

The rest of the year it is worth finding for its shape. A single katsura here has split into three trunks low down, measuring 168, 189 and 158 centimetres round, and carried all three to 25 metres. Poland registered it as a natural monument on 15 March 1992 under number 838, describing it in Polish as grujecznik japonski trojpienny: the three-trunked Japanese katsura. The register is not usually that literal, and in this case the description is all the recognition anybody needs.

There is a ceiling on how old it can be. Cercidiphyllum japonicum was unknown to Western collections until after 1865, so no katsura anywhere in Europe is much more than a century and a half old, whatever the trunks suggest. Nobody has dated this one and the register carries girths rather than birthdays. The smell, at least, arrives on schedule.

best_time.label: October, when the leaves turn and the fallen ones smell of burnt sugar

name: The Giant Thuja of Park Oliwski
age_estimate: not documented; girth suggests a mature 19th or early-20th-century planting

location.address: Park Oliwski im. Adama Mickiewicza, Oliwa, Gdansk

access: Free, public park (11.3 ha, listed historic monument), open daily in daylight hours
transport: Oliwa district; about a 12 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the drooping, scale-leaved foliage on a trunk 219 centimetres round, 23 metres tall. It stands in a tight group of four with two yews and a Nootka cypress, all protected under one register number.
story:
Poland protects four trees on this spot as a single object. A western red cedar, two common yews and a Nootka cypress grow within a few metres of one another in the dendrological corner of Park Oliwski, and the register took all of them on 15 March 1992 under one number, 836, rather than four.

The cedar is the one to stand in front of. Its trunk is 219 centimetres round and it carries 23 metres of dense, drooping, scale-leaved foliage; Gdansk's survey of its protected trees singles out the giant thujas of Park Oliwski as one of the collection's standouts, and this is the one that clears two metres of girth. Its neighbours in the record are smaller: the yews at 148 and 104 centimetres, the Nootka cypress at 143.

Thuja plicata is not a European tree at all. It belongs to the wet Pacific coast of North America, from Alaska down to northern California, where on good ground it reaches heights and ages this specimen will never come near. Somebody brought it to a Baltic park and it took, which is most of what a dendrological collection was for.

Nobody recorded when that happened. The register carries a girth, a height and a date of protection, and no birthday. If you have found a planting record for this corner of the park, tell us.

name: The Ivy Elm of Park Oliwski

location.address: Park Oliwski im. Adama Mickiewicza, by the pond, Oliwa, Gdansk

access: Free, public park (11.3 ha, listed historic monument), open daily in daylight hours
transport: Oliwa district; about a 12 minute walk from Gdansk Oliwa railway station
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the flowering ivy growing up the trunk, which is 420 centimetres round. It stands by the pond in Park Oliwski, not the willow at the Kupaly-Subislawa pond a kilometre away.
story:
Most of Europe's big elms are dead. Dutch elm disease killed them by the tens of millions across the twentieth century, which is why a European white elm with a trunk 420 centimetres round and a crown at 30 metres is now a genuinely rare thing to walk up to. This one stands by the pond in Park Oliwski and has been protected since 1 July 1988, which makes it one of the older entries on Gdansk's register.

It is not registered under its own name. Poland's entry, number 576, calls it wiaz z kwitnacym bluszczem pospolitym: an elm with flowering common ivy. The ivy going up the trunk is part of what is protected. Ivy only flowers once it has climbed high enough to reach real light, which takes decades, and when it does it flowers in autumn, weeks after everything else has finished, pulling wasps and late bees onto a tree nothing else is visiting. Standing under it in October you hear it before you work out what you are hearing.

Nobody has counted the rings. An elm of this girth is usually put somewhere between 150 and 250 years old, and that band comes from the trunk rather than from any document, so take it as the wide guess it is. What is not a guess is that the tree outlived the epidemic that took nearly every elm its size on the continent.

best_time.label: late September into October, when the ivy up the trunk flowers and the whole trunk hums
